titles.topic: Physical Properties of the Group 17 Elements
titles.subtopic: Physical Properties of the Group 17 Elements

blocks.md:
- The Group 17 elements are called **halogens**
- The halogens have uses in water purification as bleaching agents (chlorine), as flame-retardants and fire extinguishers (bromine) and as antiseptic and disinfectant agents (iodine)
- All halogens have distinct **colours **which get **darker **going down the group

blocks.text: The colours and states of the Group 17 elements

blocks.alt: Four coloured test tubes: yellow for F₂ (pale yellow gas), green for Cl₂ (green/yellow gas), orange for Br₂ (orange/brown liquid), purple for I₂ (grey/black solid).
blocks.caption: The colours of the Group 17 elements get darker going down the group

blocks.md:
- **Volatility **refers to how easily a substance can evaporate

  - A volatile substance will have a low melting and boiling point

blocks.text: Melting & boiling points of the Group 17 elements

blocks.alt: Bar chart showing the melting and boiling points of halogens. Fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is liquid, iodine and astatine are solids.
blocks.caption: The melting & boiling points of the Group 17 elements increase going down the group which indicates that the elements become less volatile

blocks.md:
- *** ***Going down the group, the **boiling point **of the elements increases which means that the **volatility **of the halogens decreases

  - This means that fluorine is the most volatile and iodine the least volatile

blocks.name: Trends in Bond Strength of Group 17

blocks.text: Trends in Bond Strength of Group 17

blocks.md:
- Halogens are **diatomic **molecules in which **covalent bonds **are formed by overlapping their orbitals
- In a covalent bond, the **bonding pair **of electrons is attracted to the nuclei on either side and it is this attraction that holds the molecule together
- Going down the group, the atomic size of the halogens **increases**
- The bonding pair of electrons get further away from the halogen nucleus and are therefore less strongly attracted towards in

blocks.alt: Diagram showing strong and weak bonds; electrons close to nuclei strengthen bonds, while further away weakens them. Labels: nucleus, inner electrons.
blocks.caption: A covalent bond is formed by the orbital overlap of two atoms and the attraction of electrons towards the nuclei; the bigger the atom, the weaker the covalent bond

blocks.md: - The bond strength of the halogen molecules therefore decreases going down the group

blocks.alt: Bar chart of bond energy in kJ per mol for F-F, Cl-Cl, Br-Br and I-I. Cl-Cl is the highest, then Br-Br; F-F and I-I are the lowest, with F-F slightly higher than I-I.
blocks.caption: The bond energies of Cl-Cl, Br-Br and I-I decrease, indicating that the bond strengths decrease going down the group

blocks.md:
- Bond energy is the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state
- The higher the bond energy, the stronger the bond
- An exception to this is **fluorine** which has a smaller bond energy than chlorine and bromine
- Fluorine is so small that when two atoms of fluorine get together their **lone** **pairs** get so close that they cause significant **repulsion** counteracting the attracting between the bonding pair of electrons and two nuclei

blocks.alt: Diagram showing electron pairs around atoms; labelled lone pairs cause repulsion and bonding pair is shown. Text explains repulsion between lone pairs.
blocks.caption: The lone pairs of fluorine get so close to each other in a fluorine molecule that they cause repulsion which decreases the bond strength

blocks.md:
- Halogens are non-metals and are **diatomic molecules **at room temperature

  - This means that they exist as molecules which are made up of two similar atoms, such as F<sub>2</sub>
- The halogens are **simple molecular structures **with **weak **van der Waals’ forces between the diatomic molecules caused by instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces

blocks.text: Electron distribution in a nonpolar molecule

blocks.alt: Diagram showing I2 molecule with even electron distribution, leading to instantaneous dipole. This induces a dipole in another I2 molecule.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows that a sudden distribution of electrons in a nonpolar molecule can cause an instantaneous dipole. When this molecule gets close to another non-polar molecule it can induce a dipole as the cloud of electrons repel the electrons in the neighbouring molecule to the other side

blocks.md:
- The more **electrons **there are in a molecule, the greater the instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces
- Therefore, the **larger **the molecule the **stronger **the van der Waals’ forces between molecules
- This is why as you go down the group, it gets more difficult to separate the molecules and the **melting **and **boiling points **increase
- As it gets more difficult to separate the molecules, the **volatility **of the halogens **decreases **going down the group

blocks.text: Van der Waals' forces and volatility in Group 17

blocks.alt: Diagram of halogen molecules (F, Cl, Br, I) showing δ+ and δ- charges, with an arrow indicating increased van der Waals’ forces and decreased volatility.
blocks.caption: Going down the group, the van der Waals’ forces increase due to an increased number of electrons in the molecules which means that the volatility decreases

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md: Instantaneous dipole – induced dipole (id–id) forces, also called London dispersion forces, are a type of van der Waals’ forces.
